prompt: A command line names a command, then a setting that changes how it behaves, then a file. Which part is the thing being acted on?
optionA: The command name
optionB: The file
optionC: The setting
optionD: All three equally
correctAnswerText: The file
explanation: The command says what to do and the setting adjusts how, leaving the file as what it is done to. The three parts have distinct roles.

prompt: What is the purpose of a setting given on a command line?
optionA: To name what the command acts on
optionB: To say where the output should go
optionC: To name the user running the command
optionD: To change how the command behaves
correctAnswerText: To change how the command behaves
explanation: A setting adjusts behaviour and does not supply the target. Confusing the two is what makes a command act on nothing or on the wrong thing.

prompt: A command line lists three file names after the command. What does that usually mean?
optionA: The command acts on all three
optionB: The command acts on the first and ignores the rest
optionC: The command acts on the last only
optionD: The command will refuse, since it expects one file
correctAnswerText: The command acts on all three
explanation: Most commands accept several targets and act on each. That is what makes a pattern expanding to many names work at all.

prompt: Why does the order of the parts on a command line matter?
optionA: Because commands run their parts left to right as separate steps
optionB: Because the last part is always ignored
optionC: Because the command has to be named first and its targets identified as targets
optionD: It does not matter; the parts can be given in any order
correctAnswerText: Because the command has to be named first and its targets identified as targets
explanation: The command name comes first because it decides how everything after it is read. Settings and targets are then distinguished by their form.

prompt: A user means to act on a file named in a certain way and the command reports that it cannot find a file with that name, while also behaving unusually. The name resembles the form a setting takes. What has most likely happened?
optionA: The file has been deleted
optionB: The name was read as a setting rather than as a target
optionC: The command does not accept targets
optionD: The command was misspelled
correctAnswerText: The name was read as a setting rather than as a target
explanation: A target that looks like a setting is read as one, so the command adjusts its behaviour and finds no target at all. Files whose names begin like settings need marking as targets explicitly.

prompt: A command is given a file name with no path. Where does it look for the file?
optionA: In the user home directory always
optionB: In the directory where the command itself is installed
optionC: Everywhere on the machine
optionD: In the directory the session is currently in
correctAnswerText: In the directory the session is currently in
explanation: A bare name is read from wherever the session happens to be. That location is a property of the session rather than of the command.

prompt: Is the current directory a property of the session or of the command being run?
optionA: Of the session
optionB: Of the command
optionC: Of the user account
optionD: Of the machine
correctAnswerText: Of the session
explanation: The session carries a current directory and every command run from it inherits that. Two sessions on the same machine can be in different places.

prompt: Two terminal sessions are open on one machine. Must they be in the same directory?
optionA: Yes; the machine has one current directory
optionB: Yes, if the same user opened both
optionC: No; each keeps its own current directory
optionD: Only if both are running commands
correctAnswerText: No; each keeps its own current directory
explanation: Each session tracks its own location independently. Moving around in one has no effect on the other.

prompt: A user runs a command that works, moves to a different directory, and runs the identical command line, which now fails. Nothing on disk has changed. What explains it?
optionA: The command was corrupted by the move
optionB: The bare names in the command resolved to different places from the two directories
optionC: The command can only be run once per session
optionD: The second directory has different permissions on the command
correctAnswerText: The bare names in the command resolved to different places from the two directories
explanation: The command line is identical and what it names is not, because bare names depend on where they are read from. Using paths that begin at the top removes the dependence.

prompt: A user wants a second copy of a file, keeping the original. Which kind of command does that?
optionA: One that moves
optionB: One that removes
optionC: One that lists
optionD: One that copies
correctAnswerText: One that copies
explanation: Copying leaves the original where it was and creates a second. Moving would relocate the one file rather than producing two.

prompt: A user wants to give a file a different name in the same directory. Which kind of command does that?
optionA: One that moves
optionB: One that copies
optionC: One that removes
optionD: One that inspects
correctAnswerText: One that moves
explanation: Renaming and relocating are the same operation: the entry changes and no second copy appears. Copying would leave the old name in place as well.

prompt: A user wants to see what a text file contains without changing it. Which kind of command does that?
optionA: One that lists names in a directory
optionB: One that copies the file
optionC: One that displays contents
optionD: One that changes the file permissions
correctAnswerText: One that displays contents
explanation: Displaying contents and listing names answer different questions. A listing tells you the file is there and nothing about what is in it.

prompt: A user wants to know which files in a directory were changed most recently. Which kind of command answers that?
optionA: One that displays the contents of each file
optionB: One that lists names together with their details
optionC: One that copies the directory somewhere else
optionD: One that searches inside the files for text
correctAnswerText: One that lists names together with their details
explanation: The question is about the entries rather than the contents, so a detailed listing answers it. Opening every file would answer a different question slowly.

prompt: A session starts in /home/asha, moves into reports, and then moves up one level. Where is it?
optionA: /home/asha/reports
optionB: /home
optionD: /home/asha
correctAnswerText: /home/asha
explanation: Moving in and then back up returns to the starting point, which is /home/asha. One further move up would have reached the directory above it.

prompt: A session starts in /var/log, moves up two levels, and then moves into tmp. Where is it?
optionA: /tmp
optionB: /var/tmp
optionC: /var/log/tmp
optionD: /tmp/log
correctAnswerText: /tmp
explanation: Two levels up from /var/log reaches the top of the tree, and entering tmp from there gives /tmp. Climbing only one level would have left the session inside /var.

prompt: A plain listing of a directory produces no output. What follows?
optionA: The directory is definitely empty
optionB: The directory does not exist
optionC: Nothing was shown, which does not establish that the directory is empty
optionD: The user lacks permission to read it
correctAnswerText: Nothing was shown, which does not establish that the directory is empty
explanation: Entries whose names mark them as hidden are left out of a plain listing. An empty result and an empty directory are different things.

prompt: A directory contains a subdirectory holding four files. A plain listing of the directory shows one entry. Why?
optionA: The listing failed to read the subdirectory
optionB: A listing shows what is in the directory, and the subdirectory is one entry
optionC: The four files are hidden
optionD: The listing shows only the first entry
correctAnswerText: A listing shows what is in the directory, and the subdirectory is one entry
explanation: The subdirectory is a single entry however much is inside it. Reaching inside is a separate request.

prompt: A file is moved from one directory to another. What exists afterwards?
optionA: Two files, one in each directory
optionB: One file, in the old directory
optionC: Two files, both in the new directory
optionD: One file, in the new directory
correctAnswerText: One file, in the new directory
explanation: Moving relocates the single file rather than duplicating it. Copying is what would leave two.

prompt: A file called report.txt is copied into a directory that already contains a different file called report.txt. What is the likely result?
optionA: The existing file is replaced by the copy, and its previous contents are gone
optionB: The copy is refused because the name is taken
optionC: The copy is renamed automatically to avoid the clash
optionD: Both files exist afterwards under the same name
correctAnswerText: The existing file is replaced by the copy, and its previous contents are gone
explanation: Most such commands overwrite without asking. Two entries cannot share one name in a directory, so one of them has to go.

prompt: A user copies notes.txt into a backup directory each evening. Tonight the backup directory already holds a notes.txt from last night, which they wanted to keep. The copy replaces any file of the same name in the destination, and both files are called notes.txt. What happens to last night version?
optionA: It is kept, since the two came from different days
optionB: It is renamed automatically before the copy arrives
optionC: It is replaced and its contents are lost
optionD: The copy is refused, leaving last night version intact
correctAnswerText: It is replaced and its contents are lost
explanation: Nothing about the file records which day it came from, so the name is all the command sees. Including a date in the destination name is what would keep both.

prompt: A directory contains a.txt, b.txt, c.log and notes.txt. A pattern matching anything ending in .txt is used. Which entries are selected?
optionA: a.txt and b.txt only
optionB: a.txt, b.txt and notes.txt
optionC: Every entry in the directory
optionD: c.log only
correctAnswerText: a.txt, b.txt and notes.txt
explanation: The pattern selects by name and every name ending in .txt qualifies, including the longer one. The log file does not.

prompt: A directory contains report.txt, report1.txt, report2.txt and a subdirectory called reports holding three more .txt files. A pattern matching anything ending in .txt is used. Which entries are selected?
optionA: All six .txt files, including those in the subdirectory
optionB: Only report.txt, since the others have digits
optionC: The subdirectory as well, since its name begins with report
optionD: The three .txt files in this directory, and none of those inside the subdirectory
correctAnswerText: The three .txt files in this directory, and none of those inside the subdirectory
explanation: A pattern of this kind selects entries in the directory it is applied to and does not descend. The subdirectory name does not end in .txt.

prompt: A directory contains data.csv, data_old.csv, .data_hidden.csv and archive.csv. A user applies a pattern matching anything beginning with data. A general pattern does not match names beginning with a dot, and one of the four begins with one. Which entries are selected?
optionA: data.csv and data_old.csv
optionB: data.csv, data_old.csv and .data_hidden.csv
optionC: data.csv only
optionD: All four entries
correctAnswerText: data.csv and data_old.csv
explanation: Names beginning with a dot are excluded from ordinary patterns deliberately, so the hidden file is left out. Archive.csv does not begin with data.

prompt: A file is removed with a command that deletes it. Where does it go?
optionA: To a recycle bin, from which it can be restored
optionB: To a temporary directory for a period
optionC: Nowhere; it is gone and there is no bin to recover it from
optionD: To the directory above, renamed
correctAnswerText: Nowhere; it is gone and there is no bin to recover it from
explanation: A command-line removal does not pass through a bin. Recovery afterwards depends on a backup having been taken.

prompt: A directory contains four files. A removal command is applied with a pattern matching anything ending in .tmp, and three of the four end in .tmp. What is lost?
optionA: All four files
optionB: The three .tmp files, without any confirmation being asked
optionC: Nothing, until the user confirms
optionD: The three .tmp files, after a confirmation prompt
correctAnswerText: The three .tmp files, without any confirmation being asked
explanation: The pattern selects three names and the command acts on each. Nothing asks first unless it has been set up to.

prompt: A user means to remove files ending in .bak and types a pattern that matches everything instead. The directory holds twelve files, three of them .bak. The pattern selects all twelve names and the command acts on each without asking. What is lost?
optionA: The three .bak files only
optionB: Nothing, since the pattern was clearly a mistake
optionC: The three .bak files, with the rest reported as errors
optionD: All twelve files
correctAnswerText: All twelve files
explanation: The command has no way to know which of the twelve were intended. Listing what a pattern matches before removing is the habit this exists to justify.

prompt: A command is told to work throughout a tree, starting at a directory. How far does it reach?
optionA: Everything below that directory, at every depth
optionB: Only the immediate contents
optionC: Only the directories, not the files
optionD: Only two levels down
correctAnswerText: Everything below that directory, at every depth
explanation: Working throughout a tree means every level below the starting point. Depth is not limited unless something limits it.

prompt: A directory holds two files and one subdirectory. That subdirectory holds three files and another subdirectory holding one file. A command working throughout the tree is applied to the top directory. How many files does it reach?
optionA: Two
optionB: Five
optionC: Six
optionD: Three
correctAnswerText: Six
explanation: Two at the top, three in the first subdirectory and one deeper: Six in all. Counting only the entries directly inside the starting directory would give a much smaller answer.

prompt: A user applies a removal command throughout a tree, meaning to clear one subdirectory, and gives the parent directory by mistake. The parent holds nine files of its own and four subdirectories. Working throughout a tree reaches every level below the directory given, and the directory given was the parent. What is lost?
optionA: Only the one subdirectory that was intended
optionB: The nine files, all four subdirectories and everything inside them
optionC: The nine files only, with the subdirectories left alone
optionD: The four subdirectories only, with the nine files left alone
correctAnswerText: The nine files, all four subdirectories and everything inside them
explanation: Naming the parent hands the command the whole tree beneath it. This single mistake is the reason for listing what a command would reach before running it.

prompt: A file is named "my report.txt", with a space in the middle. It is given to a command unquoted. What does the command receive?
optionA: One target, "my report.txt"
optionB: One target, "myreport.txt"
optionC: Nothing, since the name is invalid
optionD: Two separate targets, "my" and "report.txt"
correctAnswerText: Two separate targets, "my" and "report.txt"
explanation: A space separates one part of a command line from the next, so the name arrives as two. Quoting is what keeps it together.

prompt: A removal command is given the unquoted name "old notes.txt" in a directory that happens to contain a file called old and a file called notes.txt. What is removed?
optionA: Both old and notes.txt
optionB: Nothing, since no file is called old notes.txt
optionC: Only the file called old
optionD: A file called oldnotes.txt, if one exists
correctAnswerText: Both old and notes.txt
explanation: The command receives two names, both of which exist, and removes both. It succeeds completely and does entirely the wrong thing.

prompt: A script builds a file name from a value that sometimes contains a space, and passes it unquoted to a command. Most of the time the value has no space and the script works. An unquoted value containing a space arrives as two separate targets rather than one. What happens on the day it does?
optionA: The command fails and the script stops
optionB: The command acts on the first part and ignores the second
optionC: The command acts on two things instead of one, and reports success
optionD: The script refuses to build the name
correctAnswerText: The command acts on two things instead of one, and reports success
explanation: Nothing detects the split, so the failure is silent and intermittent. That the script has worked for months is exactly what makes the day it does not so confusing.

prompt: A command reports that a file does not exist. The user can see the file listed in a window on the same machine. What is the most likely explanation?
optionA: The file was deleted a moment ago
optionB: The session is in a different directory from the one being viewed
optionC: The command lacks permission to see it
optionD: The file name contains an invisible character
correctAnswerText: The session is in a different directory from the one being viewed
explanation: The command looked where the session is and the window is showing somewhere else. Both reports are accurate about different places.

prompt: A command reports that a file does not exist. A listing of the current directory shows a file whose name looks identical. The listing shows the name and the command searched the same directory, so the two names must differ in something not visible. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The session is in a different directory
optionB: The user lacks permission on the file
optionC: The command was misspelled
optionD: The two names differ in something that does not show, such as a trailing space or a differing character
correctAnswerText: The two names differ in something that does not show, such as a trailing space or a differing character
explanation: Being in the wrong directory is ruled out by the stem, which leaves the names themselves. Names that look identical and differ invisibly are a genuine and maddening case.

prompt: A user intends to act on files beginning with log and finds that a directory called logs was affected too. Why?
optionA: The pattern matched the directory name as well, since it also begins with log
optionB: Directories are always included regardless of the pattern
optionC: The command treats directories as files
optionD: The directory was affected by a different command
correctAnswerText: The pattern matched the directory name as well, since it also begins with log
explanation: A pattern matches names, and a directory has a name like anything else. Nothing about being a directory exempts it.

prompt: A user applies a pattern intending to select three files and twelve entries are affected. The directory contains twelve entries in total. The pattern matched every entry in the directory rather than the three intended. What does that indicate about the pattern?
optionA: It matched only files and there were twelve files
optionB: It matched the three intended files three times each
optionC: It was general enough to match every name present
optionD: The command ignored the pattern entirely
correctAnswerText: It was general enough to match every name present
explanation: Twelve of twelve is the signature of a pattern that constrains nothing. Listing what a pattern expands to before acting is what turns this into a non-event.

prompt: A user is about to remove files matching a pattern and wants to know first what would go. What should they do?
optionA: Run the removal and watch what happens
optionB: Apply the same pattern to a command that only lists
optionC: Take a backup of the directory
optionD: Remove the files one at a time
correctAnswerText: Apply the same pattern to a command that only lists
explanation: Listing with the identical pattern shows exactly the set the removal would act on. A backup is a good habit and answers a different question.

prompt: A user plans a destructive command and takes a full backup first. A colleague says they should still list what the command would affect. A backup allows recovery afterwards and does not show what the command would act on beforehand. Is the colleague right?
optionA: No; the backup makes the listing unnecessary
optionB: No; listing and backing up achieve the same thing
optionC: Yes, but only if the backup might be incomplete
optionD: Yes; the backup allows recovery and does not tell them what is about to happen
correctAnswerText: Yes; the backup allows recovery and does not tell them what is about to happen
explanation: Recovering from a mistake and avoiding one are different goods, and the backup only offers the first. Noticing that a pattern matches twelve things rather than three costs nothing.

prompt: A user lists what a pattern matches, sees the expected three files, and then runs the removal ten minutes later. In the intervening ten minutes another process created four more files matching the same pattern. What happens?
optionA: Seven files are removed, since the pattern is evaluated again when the removal runs
optionB: Three files are removed, as listed
optionC: Three files are removed and the four new ones are reported as errors
optionD: The removal is refused because the directory changed
correctAnswerText: Seven files are removed, since the pattern is evaluated again when the removal runs
explanation: The listing described the directory at the moment it ran, and the pattern is expanded afresh. On a directory something else writes to, the gap between checking and acting is the risk.

prompt: A team wants a script to remove old files safely. A colleague proposes having it print what it would remove and do nothing, until somebody has read the output. Printing without acting lets the set be checked before anything is destroyed. What does the proposal buy?
optionA: Nothing; the script will remove the same files either way
optionB: A guarantee that the right files are removed
optionC: The chance to see the set before anything is destroyed, at the cost of a second run
optionD: Protection against the directory changing between the two runs
correctAnswerText: The chance to see the set before anything is destroyed, at the cost of a second run
explanation: It buys review and guarantees nothing, since the set can change between the two runs. That remaining gap is why this is a safeguard rather than a proof.

prompt: A user is about to run a destructive command and cannot decide whether the risk justifies the time spent checking. The command would act on a directory holding work that exists nowhere else. The material exists in no other copy, so a mistake could not be undone. What follows?
optionA: The check is unnecessary, since the command is simple
optionB: The check is worth its cost, since a mistake here cannot be undone
optionC: The check is unnecessary if the user is experienced
optionD: The command should not be run at all
correctAnswerText: The check is worth its cost, since a mistake here cannot be undone
explanation: Irreversibility is what makes checking worth the time rather than the complexity of the command. The same command against a directory with a backup would be a different decision.

prompt: A user must place a file in a second directory while keeping it available in the first. The file must remain in the original directory and must also be present in the second. Which command fits?
optionA: One that moves
optionB: One that removes and recreates
optionC: One that renames
optionD: One that copies
correctAnswerText: One that copies
explanation: Keeping both requires a duplicate, which is what copying produces. Moving satisfies the second requirement and breaks the first.

prompt: A user must clear temporary files from a directory that also holds work in progress. The temporary files all end in .tmp and no file of value ends in .tmp. Only .tmp files are to go and no valuable file carries that ending. Which approach fits?
optionA: A removal restricted to a pattern matching .tmp, applied to that directory only
optionB: A removal applied throughout the tree, to be thorough
optionC: A removal of everything, followed by restoring the work in progress
optionD: Removing the files one by one after inspecting each
correctAnswerText: A removal restricted to a pattern matching .tmp, applied to that directory only
explanation: The pattern is exactly as wide as the requirement. Working throughout the tree reaches directories nobody mentioned, and inspecting each by hand is unnecessary given the stated rule.

prompt: A user must remove a directory and everything in it. A colleague suggests removing the files first and then the directory, to be careful. Working throughout the tree does both in one step and reaches the same set of things. What is the difference between the two approaches?
optionA: The careful route destroys less
optionB: The careful route is safer because it can be stopped partway
optionC: None in what is destroyed; the careful route only makes the set visible along the way
optionD: The single command destroys more than the careful route
correctAnswerText: None in what is destroyed; the careful route only makes the set visible along the way
explanation: Both end with the same directory gone. What the slower route offers is the chance to notice something unexpected before it is too late, and it can indeed be stopped partway — which is a reason to prefer it and not a difference in reach.

prompt: A user must rename two hundred files according to a rule. They can do it by hand or write a short loop. The rule is mechanical and applies to every one of the two hundred files in the same way. Which fits?
optionA: By hand, since a loop might affect the wrong files
optionB: The loop, since the rule is uniform and two hundred repetitions invite mistakes
optionC: By hand, since two hundred is not many
optionD: The loop, but only after renaming ten by hand first
correctAnswerText: The loop, since the rule is uniform and two hundred repetitions invite mistakes
explanation: Uniformity is what makes the work automatable and repetition is what makes doing it by hand error-prone. Testing the loop on a copy first is a sensible refinement rather than a reason to avoid it.

prompt: A user must free space and can either remove old files or move them to slower storage. The files are needed a few times a year and cannot be regenerated. The files cannot be regenerated and are still wanted occasionally. Which fits?
optionA: Removing them, since they are used only a few times a year
optionB: Removing them, since space is the stated problem
optionC: Leaving them where they are
optionD: Moving them to slower storage, since they are still wanted and cannot be recreated
correctAnswerText: Moving them to slower storage, since they are still wanted and cannot be recreated
explanation: Both facts point the same way: still wanted rules out removal and irreproducible makes removal irreversible. Rarity of use is an argument about where they live rather than whether they should exist.

prompt: A command is documented as acting on every entry below the directory it is given, following the tree to any depth, and as asking for no confirmation. A user gives it their home directory. It follows the tree to any depth from the directory given and asks for no confirmation. What would it act on?
optionA: Everything anywhere below their home directory
optionB: Only the entries directly inside their home directory
optionC: Only the files, leaving the directories alone
optionD: Nothing, until the user confirms
correctAnswerText: Everything anywhere below their home directory
explanation: The documented behaviour settles it without any need to recognise the command. Reading what a command says it does is what makes an unfamiliar one safe to reason about.

prompt: A command is documented as taking a source and a destination, and as replacing the destination if it exists. A user gives it two file names by mistake in the wrong order. The command replaces whatever is at the destination, and the two names were supplied the wrong way round. What happens?
optionA: The command refuses, since the order is wrong
optionB: The command detects the mistake and swaps them
optionC: The file they meant to keep is replaced by the one they meant to overwrite
optionD: Both files are left unchanged
correctAnswerText: The file they meant to keep is replaced by the one they meant to overwrite
explanation: The command cannot know which order was intended, and both names are valid in either position. The documented replacement behaviour is what makes the mistake destructive rather than harmless.

prompt: A command is documented as expanding any pattern it is given before acting, and as acting on every resulting name. A user gives it a pattern in a directory they have not looked at. The pattern is expanded against a directory whose contents the user has not seen. What is the safest next step?
optionA: Run the command, since the pattern was written carefully
optionB: List what the pattern expands to in that directory before running the command
optionC: Run the command from a different directory
optionD: Give the command a single file name instead of the pattern
correctAnswerText: List what the pattern expands to in that directory before running the command
explanation: The pattern is precise and the directory is unknown, so what it selects is unknown. Listing first converts an unknown set into a visible one.

prompt: A command is documented as reporting success whether or not it found anything to act on. A script uses it and treats success as meaning the work was done. Success is reported even when nothing was found, so a successful result does not establish that anything happened. What is wrong with the script?
optionA: Nothing; success means the command ran correctly
optionB: The command should be replaced, since reporting success is misleading
optionC: The script should run the command twice to be certain
optionD: It cannot distinguish work done from nothing found, since both report success
correctAnswerText: It cannot distinguish work done from nothing found, since both report success
explanation: The command is behaving exactly as documented, which is why reading the documentation matters here. Checking that the expected change actually occurred is what the script has to do instead.
